## Goals for today

::: {.nonincremental}
1. Learn about three advanced object types: **`factor`**, **`data.frame`** and
   **`tibble`**
2. Understand their **relation to the basic types** discussed previously
:::

# Part I: Where the advanced types fit {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## The picture, extended

::: {.mermaid-tight}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  V["Vectors"] --> A["Atomic vectors"]
```

:::

## On more advanced object types

- There are many object types in R, but **understanding the basics is key**
  - They are by far the most common ones
  - All other object types are somehow *built upon* the basic types by adding
    **attributes**

::: {.columns .smaller}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Categorical data: `factor`**

- Takes one out of a pre-specified number of values: **levels**
- Classical example: male, female, diverse
- Created with `factor()`
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**Data frames: `data.frame` & `tibble`**

- A kind of *table* in which different variables are stored as vectors
- `tibble`s are a modern variant that "do less and complain more"
- Created with `data.frame()` / `tibble::tibble()`
:::
:::

::: {.tiny .muted}
Others we will not cover: matrices, durations, dates
:::

## Digression: attributes

- To turn basic types into something fancier we give them **attributes**, one of
  which is called **`class`**
  - This changes their behaviour when functions are applied to them
  - Technically, adding a class attribute changes the **class**, not the **type**:

::: {.small}
```r
ff <- factor(c("F", "M", "M"), levels = c("F", "M", "D"))
typeof(ff)   # integer
class(ff)    # factor
attributes(ff)
```
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The class `factor` is an **integer** with two attributes: `levels` and `class`
:::

# Part II: Factors {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## Factors

- Factors represent **ordinal or categorical data**
  - Elements can take one out of several pre-specified values: **levels**
  - Factors are integers with the attributes `levels` and `class`
- Created with `factor()`, which takes a vector and an optional argument `levels`:

::: {.small}
```r
f_1 <- factor(c(rep("F", 4), rep("D", 5), rep("M", 3)),
              levels = c("D", "F", "M"))
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="default"}
## Your turn
- What happens if we do **not** specify `levels` explicitly?
- What happens if the vector contains elements **not** pre-specified as levels?
:::

## Ordered factors and `table()`

- Usually levels are **not ordered** — for ordinal data use the argument
  `ordered`:

::: {.small}
```r
f_2 <- factor(c("high", "high", "low"),
              levels = c("low", "mid", "high"),
              ordered = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="default"}
## What does `table()` do?
Try it on the factors you defined so far. How can you make sure that the
frequency of elements which do not show up in the vector is displayed as zero?
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="default"}
## A remark on using factors in practice
In my experience it is usually better to store categorical data as **character**,
and only transform them into factors if necessary
:::

# Part III: Data frames and tibbles {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## Data frames

::: {.takeaway}
Data frames are **special lists of vectors** where the length of each vector is
equal — so most list operations also work for data frames
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.small}
```
  gender height
1   male    189
2   male    175
3   male    180
4 female    166
5 female    150
```
:::

::: {.tiny .muted}
column names = names of the vectors · each column = one vector
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.small}
```r
df_1 <- data.frame(
  "gender" = c(rep("male", 3), rep("female", 2)),
  "height" = c(189, 175, 180, 166, 150)
)
```
:::

To create a data frame from a list, use `as.data.frame()`
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
Data read into R almost always starts off as a `data.frame` → transforming them
is the subject of the **data wrangling** sessions
:::

## Data frames and tibbles

- A modern version of the `data.frame` is the **`tibble`** (package *tibble*)
  - We mostly use tibbles, but familiarise yourself with the differences to the
    `data.frame`, which remains widespread → tutorial reading
- Transform a `data.frame` (or a `list`) into a tibble:

::: {.small}
```r
tb_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(df_1)
```
:::

- To extract single columns use `[` or `[[`
  - What is the difference between the two?
  - How do you test for the type of a column vector?

## Getting an overview, and R dialects

- Quick overview of the content: `dplyr::glimpse()` or `head()`
- Complete overview: `View()`
- Data frames are among the **most widely used** data types
  - Different approaches to handling them, each associated with an R **dialect**
  - We mainly use the **tidyverse** dialect — easiest to learn and comprehend,
    built upon **tibbles**
  - Alternatives: **base** (classical) and **data.table** (fastest), which mainly
    use `data.frame`s and `data.table`s

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Useful to keep in mind when searching for help on the internet
:::

## Final exercises {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

::: {.nonincremental}
- Create a **factor** with the levels `"still"`, `"medium"`, `"sparkling"` and
  arbitrary instances of the three levels
- Get the **relative frequencies** for `"medium"` of this factor
- Create a **data frame** with two columns: `"nb"` containing the numbers `1` to
  `5` as *double*, and `"char"` containing the numbers `6` to `10` as *character*
- Transform this data frame into a **tibble**
- Extract the second column of this tibble such that you obtain a **vector**
:::
